newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-TIGER WOODS CAN AFFORD TO PLAY AT HIS OWN PACE, FATHER SAYS.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-TIGER WOODS CAN AFFORD TO PLAY AT HIS OWN PACE, FATHER SAYS.

text.p: Tournament organisers are clamouring for Tiger Woods to play their events, but golf's $60 million superstar can afford to play at his own pace and for his own place in golf history, according to his father and advisor Earl Woods.

"We are not greedy. Money is not important. None of this is about money," said the elder Woods, who Thursday signed copies of his new book, 'Training a Tiger. A Father's Guide to Raising a Winner in both Golf and Life' at the All-Star Cafe.
"It's about letting Tiger be the best that he can be."

Woods, who reaped a $60 million bonanza in sponsorship deals after he turned pro, has not played since his spectacular triumph in the Masters on April 13 and is not expected to play again on the tour until May 15 at the Byron Nelson Classic in Irving, Texas.

"After a major energy expenditure, Tiger needs time to regroup," said the elder Woods, who sat his son in a high chair at 6 months of age to watch father practice his swing. By the time Tiger was 8, he was winning international junior events.

The long-hitting Woods, an unprecedented three-time winner of both the U.S. Amateur and U.S. Junior championships, exploded on the pro scene last summer after leaving Stanford University and won three of hi events on the tour.
In his first crack at the Masters as a professional, Woods became the youngest champion (age 21), set a tournament scoring record (18 under par) and won by the widest margin (12 shots).

Woods's phenomenal success in majors is keyed to his preparation, focus and ability to peak at the right time, says father Woods. The first black player to win a Grand Slam golf event has already learned some lessons on the PGA Tour.
"Myself, his agent Hughes Norton (of IMG) and Tiger map out the schedule," the proud father said. "We do it in thirds (of the season). That priority is first and foremost.
"In the first third of this year, we found that he can not handle four tournaments in a row. You will not see that in the near future."
Woods, a Vietnam veteran as a Green Beret who had heart bypass surgery about two months ago, said his son will gear his game for the majors.
Next up is the U.S. Open at Congressional in Bethesda, Maryland, starting on June 12.
"There's no frenzy to schedule him after a major performance and leading up to a major performance he always takes one or two weeks off," said Woods.

"As we go through the schedule, we'll continue to evaluate his performance to see they mesh to his advantage. The tournaments he decides to play have nothing to do with tournament sites, sponsors or anything else."
Woods said his son would not be ruffled at all by the storm of criticism heaped on Fuzzy Zoeller for making ill-advised wisecracks of a racial nature following Woods's Masters win.
"Tiger is mature well beyond his years," he said.

Father Woods echoed the sentiments expressed by his son in accepting Zoeller's public apology. "Fuzzy is still a jokester. He needs a little more common sense as to when and where to tell jokes. I don't hold it against him. It was bad judgment and bad timing. Nothing personal."
As for his son's personal goals, Woods said he was in the dark.
"Tiger has not shared his goals with me, never," said Woods, before adding: "But I knew in advance he wanted to win the Masters, though, just through his actions.

"It was his extensive film study of the Masters. I have kept tapes of past Masters tournaments and he spent a great deal of time watching film. He was learning the greens, and the strategy othenquer the tournament."
